A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Feedback Friction study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original iterative-feedback experiments across nine benchmark tasks, sampling interventions, error categorization, and additional confidence, familiarity, complexity, and failure-overlap analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds semantic-entropy analyses, feedback-understanding and belief-update probes, and a prompt-format comparison.

M1.justification: The iterative solver-feedback loop, F1/F2/F3 feedback mechanisms, answer masking, and temperature/rejection-sampling procedures remain unchanged. The added confidence measurements and self-perception probes are diagnostics, rather than new components of the proposed solver procedure.

E1.justification: All benchmark datasets are retained, including the appendix's six-digit multiplication task. Section 4.3 and Appendix H add a diagnostic task requiring explicit yes/no judgments and explanations about feedback understanding and belief updating, extending the evaluated behavior beyond problem solving.

E2.justification: Section 3.1 adds an evaluated multi-turn conversation variant against the established single-prompt approach, reporting marginal differences. The original solver lineup, F1/F2/F3 comparisons, and sampling-strategy comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The main confidence analysis changes from token probabilities to semantic entropy, using 50 sampled outputs at temperature 0.7, final-answer clustering, 0.2-wide bins, and a normalized improvement metric. Its model pairing becomes Llama-3.3 and Scout rather than Scout and Maverick. New self-report and conversation-format protocols are also introduced; the original benchmark protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands the investigation of feedback resistance through semantic-entropy analyses, direct self-perception probes with a worked failure example, and a prompt-format robustness check. The original Appendix D token-confidence analysis and the familiarity, complexity, and failure-overlap analyses remain.

E5.justification: The new entropy analysis specifies 50-output sampling and displays bucket counts, with Appendix I flagging sparse regions. Its plots omit the error bars present in v1's replaced Figure 6. The binomial-standard-error convention remains stated, and no increase in independent benchmark runs is established.

E6.justification: New results report an entropy/improvement association, over 95% affirmative feedback-understanding responses, over 96% affirmative belief-update responses, and marginal prompt-format effects. Figure 6's earlier confidence results are replaced under different measurement conditions, with additional results in Figure 21. Main benchmark scores and both tables are unchanged; this is not a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for the semantic-cluster probability estimator, semantic entropy, and normalized improvement, (Final - Initial)/(1 - Initial). The existing iterative-loop, accuracy, and token-confidence definitions remain, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract changes from ruling out model overconfidence to claiming that semantic-entropy confidence predicts feedback resistance. The introduction also elevates the disconnect between stated feedback acceptance and actual behavior into a main finding. The central claim that models plateau despite helpful feedback is retained.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 now interprets confidence as associated with resistance and self-reported acceptance without correction as a self-assessment or implementation failure. This substantially changes v1's explanatory account, although the retained token-probability results concern a different confidence measure. Section 6 still acknowledges the absence of a definitive mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 documents entropy sampling, clustering and binning, conversation-role formatting, and the exact self-perception prompts in Appendix H. These support the added analyses. Existing solver hardware, original prompt templates, and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Farquhar et al.'s work on semantic entropy to motivate the new confidence analysis. ClasHEval remains cited under a different reference number. The broader related-work discussion and positioning around externally guided self-improvement are essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the abstract, introduction's findings paragraph, experimental-controls discussion, confidence analysis, and limitations. Appendices H and I are added, and the publication header changes to NeurIPS 2025. Most prose and the overall section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 6 changes from two small token-confidence panels to a full-width six-panel semantic-entropy display. New Figures 19–21 provide probe prompts, a dialogue example, and ten entropy-result panels with sample counts and sparse-region markings. Existing appendix displays are repositioned, while the other original figure contents and both tables are retained.

improvement.justification: The new controls and diagnostic analyses broaden the evidence, but a central addition has an unresolved numerical inconsistency. In v2 Figure 6, Llama-3.3/GPQA at entropy about 0.1 has initial/final accuracies near 0.69/0.93: the caption's formula implies improvement near 0.77, while the green curve is near 0.15. The PDFs do not explain this discrepancy, which undermines verification of the revised confidence claim. The useful additions and uncertainty about their central quantitative evidence prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
